title: Concurrency Bugs & Heisenbugs
summary: Some bugs vanish the instant you try to observe them. Learn why timing-dependent bugs are the hardest class to debug, the tools built specifically for them, and why "just add a sleep" is never the fix.

slides.markdown:
Every technique so far assumes a bug is stable — reproduce it, shrink it, binary-search to it, and it stays put while you investigate. Concurrency bugs break that assumption: they depend on the precise interleaving of threads, and the interleaving changes every run, sometimes every observation.

A **Heisenbug** is named for exactly this: a bug whose behavior changes when you try to measure it, the way adding a `print` statement or a debugger breakpoint can shift timing just enough to make a race stop happening — or start happening somewhere new.

This is the class of bug where the standard toolkit from [debugging-tools-techniques](debugging-tools-techniques) is least reliable, and where specialized tools and a different mental model earn their keep.

slides.sectionTitle: What makes a bug a Heisenbug
slides.markdown:
A **Heisenbug** is a bug whose behavior changes — often disappears — under the very act of observation. The name is a nod to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: measuring the system perturbs it.

Why this happens: most concurrency bugs depend on a specific, narrow window of timing where two threads touch shared state in the wrong order. Any observation tool — a `print`, a breakpoint, a profiler sampling stack traces — adds overhead and changes exactly the timing that window depends on. Slow one thread down by a few microseconds with a log statement, and the race that was happening every hundred runs stops happening at all while you're watching.

The practical consequence: **the absence of the bug while you're debugging it is not evidence the bug is fixed.** It may just mean your instrumentation nudged the timing out of the failure window, and it'll be back in production the moment you remove the logging you added to find it.

slides.subTitle: Shared state without ordering guarantees
slides.markdown:
A **race condition** exists when two or more threads access shared state, at least one write is involved, and the program's correctness depends on an ordering between them that isn't actually guaranteed.

```python
# counter starts at 0, two threads run this concurrently:
def increment():
    temp = counter        # read
    temp = temp + 1       # modify
    counter = temp        # write
```

Each thread's read-modify-write is three separate steps, not one atomic operation. If both threads read `counter` as 0 before either writes back, one increment is silently lost — the final value is 1 instead of 2. Nothing crashes; the program just produces a wrong answer, and which runs hit it depends on the scheduler's whims that day.

The fix is always the same shape: make the operation atomic (a lock, a compare-and-swap, an atomic type), not "make the race less likely." Less likely still means it happens — just at 2am on the busiest day of the year instead of in your test suite.

Seeing two threads' operations interleaved on a timeline makes it obvious why the outcome depends on scheduling: **Thread A** reads `counter=0`, then before it writes back, the scheduler switches to **Thread B**, which also reads `counter=0`, increments, and writes `counter=1`. Control returns to Thread A, which still has `temp=1` from its earlier read, increments to `1`, and writes `counter=1` again — overwriting Thread B's update. Two increments, one survives.

A different interleaving — where Thread A completes its full read-modify-write before Thread B starts — produces the correct result, `counter=2`. Same code, same inputs, two different outcomes purely from scheduling order, which is exactly why this bug is intermittent rather than deterministic.

slides.subTitle: Recognizing the symptom and the resource-ordering cause
slides.markdown:
A **deadlock**: two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, and neither will release what it holds. The symptom is unmistakable once you know it — the process is alive but frozen, CPU usage often near zero, and it never recovers on its own.

The classic cause is **inconsistent lock ordering**: Thread A acquires Lock 1 then tries for Lock 2; Thread B acquires Lock 2 then tries for Lock 1. If both acquire their first lock before either reaches for the second, neither can proceed — forever. The fix is a global convention: always acquire locks in the same order everywhere in the codebase, so this circular wait can't form.

A **livelock** is the more confusing cousin: threads aren't frozen, they're actively running, but they're stuck responding to each other in a loop that never makes progress — two threads each repeatedly backing off and retrying in a way that keeps re-colliding. CPU usage is high, unlike a deadlock, which is often the first clue that distinguishes the two.

slides.subTitle: Why adding a log statement can hide a timing bug
slides.markdown:
The **probe effect** is the general name for any observation changing the behavior being observed — Heisenbugs are the symptom, the probe effect is the mechanism. Every debugging tool has a cost, and for timing-sensitive bugs that cost can be the whole story.

Concretely: a `print` statement does I/O, which is orders of magnitude slower than an in-memory operation — inserting one inside a tight race window can push the two threads' operations far enough apart in time that they simply stop colliding. A breakpoint pauses one thread while others continue, which can either mask a race (the paused thread stops competing for the resource) or, just as often, *create* a new one by holding a lock far longer than the code normally would.

The practical implication: for suspected timing bugs, **prefer the lowest-overhead observation available** — an atomic counter incremented on each access, a log written to an in-memory ring buffer flushed later, or a specialized tool built to minimize this exact distortion — over a debugger or naive logging.

Because standard tools distort timing, concurrency bugs have their own specialized toolkit:

- **Thread sanitizers** (ThreadSanitizer / TSan) instrument memory accesses at compile time to detect data races directly — two threads touching the same memory without synchronization — even if the race never actually produces a visibly wrong result on that run. This catches races before they manifest as a Heisenbug at all.
- **Deterministic replay** tools record a program's actual thread-scheduling decisions during one run, then let you replay that *exact* interleaving repeatedly — turning a bug that happens once in a thousand runs into one you can reproduce on demand.
- **Stress testing** deliberately runs concurrent code under heavy, varied load (more threads than cores, artificial delays inserted at random points) specifically to widen the odds of hitting a rare interleaving, rather than hoping normal testing stumbles onto it.

Of these, running a thread sanitizer in CI is the highest-leverage habit for a team writing concurrent code — it turns "this will probably be fine" into a build failure before the race ever ships.

slides.subTitle: Use-after-free and buffer overruns are non-deterministic too
slides.markdown:
Memory-safety bugs share the Heisenbug property even though they aren't strictly concurrency bugs: a **use-after-free** writes to memory that's already been reclaimed, and whether that write corrupts something you'll notice depends entirely on what the allocator happened to put in that freed slot next — which can differ run to run, build to build, or with something as small as adding a log statement that changes allocation patterns.

A **buffer overrun** similarly corrupts whatever memory happens to sit past the buffer's end — sometimes unused padding (silent, no symptom), sometimes a critical pointer (a crash far from the actual bug).

This is why these bugs are notorious for "disappearing" when you add debug output or run under different build flags: you haven't fixed anything, you've changed the memory layout enough that the corruption now lands somewhere harmless instead of somewhere visible. The sanitizers from [debugging-tools-techniques](debugging-tools-techniques) exist specifically because normal testing can't reliably catch this class of bug at all.

Under deadline pressure, a common "fix" for a race condition is adding a `sleep()` or delay so one thread reliably finishes before another starts. This is not a fix — it's placing a bet on a specific timing that has no guarantee behind it.

Why it fails: the sleep duration was tuned against today's hardware, today's load, and today's scheduler behavior. A busier production server, a slower CI runner, a different cloud instance type, or simply more contention next quarter can all shrink or eliminate the margin the sleep depended on — and the race comes back, usually somewhere that's harder to reproduce than the original report, since now there are two timing-dependent factors instead of one.

It also actively hides the bug from detection tools: a race "papered over" with a sleep often no longer triggers in a thread sanitizer's default test run, so it can silently pass CI while remaining exploitable under the exact conditions the sleep didn't anticipate.

The actual fix is always synchronization that provides a *guarantee*, not a probabilistic delay: a lock, an atomic operation, or a well-defined happens-before relationship (a queue, a future, a barrier).

Debugging a suspected concurrency bug calls for adjustments to the standard loop: treat "it stopped happening when I added logging" as inconclusive, not as evidence of a fix. Prefer thread sanitizers and stress testing over stepping through with a debugger, since detection tools built for races don't rely on catching the bug in the act the way a breakpoint does. When you do need to observe, prefer the lowest-overhead method available.

And hold the bar higher for "verified" — a race that didn't reproduce in 100 stress-test runs isn't proven fixed; it may need 100,000 runs, or a sanitizer that detects the race statically regardless of whether it manifested. The absence of a symptom is weak evidence for a Heisenbug in a way it isn't for most other bug classes.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this matters beyond the bug itself
slides.markdown:
Concurrency bugs are disproportionately expensive not because they're hard to fix once found — the fix is usually a lock or an atomic — but because they're hard to *find*, hard to *reproduce on demand*, and easy to *falsely believe fixed*. A team that ships a sleep-based patch and closes the ticket has, in a very real sense, made the bug worse: it's now hidden behind a false sense of resolution instead of an open, known issue.

This is also why concurrency bugs are a favorite interview topic at the advanced end — they test whether a candidate reasons about correctness from guarantees (what does the language or library actually promise?) rather than from observed behavior (it worked when I ran it), which is precisely the trap a Heisenbug sets.

This is the hardest single-engineer debugging problem in the group; the next two topics shift from individual technique to team process. [on-call-and-incident-response](on-call-and-incident-response) covers what happens when a bug like this manifests as a live incident before anyone has diagnosed it — how a team detects and triages under uncertainty. [postmortems-and-incident-learning](postmortems-and-incident-learning) covers turning a hard-won diagnosis like a rare race condition into organizational knowledge, so the next engineer who hits a similar symptom doesn't start from zero.
